The original opening date was 14 September 2026 (E3). The operator announced an 11-week delay to the public opening (E4), which is 77 days.

Counting forward from 14 September: 16 days reach 30 September, 31 more reach 31 October (47 days in total), and the remaining 30 days reach 30 November.

Weekday check: 14 September 2026 is a Monday, so adding 11 full weeks gives another Monday. 30 November 2026 is a Monday, which is consistent.

The panelist who answered 7 December 2026 appears to have miscounted by a week. 7 December would be 12 weeks after 14 September.

Answer: 30 November 2026

The original opening date was 14 September 2026 (E3). Adding the announced 11-week delay gives 30 November 2026 (E4).

Answer: 30 November 2026.

The original public opening of the Dravenholt Tunnel was scheduled for 14 September 2026 (E3). The operator subsequently announced an 11-week delay to this opening (E4). 

An 11-week delay equals 77 days (11 × 7). Counting forward 77 days from 14 September 2026:
- Remaining days in September (30 days total): 30 − 14 = 16 days (reaches 30 September).
- Days in October: 31 days (16 + 31 = 47 days, reaches 31 October).
- Remaining days to add in November: 77 − 47 = 30 days.

Adding 30 days in November brings the expected opening date to 30 November 2026 (the panelist suggesting 7 December mistakenly added 12 weeks).

Answer: 30 November 2026

Answer: 30 November 2026
